standards.name: Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (OBI)
standards.abstract: OBI (Ontology for Biomedical Investigations) is an ontology for describing scientific investigations, providing a controlled vocabulary of terms for assays, devices, study designs, data items and related concepts used in biomedical research. It is intended for use across diverse biomedical investigation modalities (laboratory assays, clinical assessments, questionnaires, sequencing, imaging, etc.) to improve clarity, integration and machine-readability of metadata. OBI is a community-developed resource maintained by the OBI consortium and follows OBO Foundry principles; it provides term submission guidelines, templates, import mechanisms, and OWL-formal logical definitions to support interoperability and reuse.

classification.rationale: The source material is primarily prose guidance, policy and submission/checklist-style instructions (term guidelines, README, documentation) rather than a field-level metadata table or an ordered process DAG. The content lists requirements and recommendations for term creation and ontology use—these are best represented as principles.

principles.principle: OBI provides a controlled vocabulary of terms for biomedical investigations (assays, devices, objectives, etc.).
principles.evidence: The Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (OBI) helps you communicate clearly about scientific investigations by defining more than 2500 terms for assays, devices, objectives, and more.

principles.principle: OBI is an ontology: a system of defined terminology with logical relationships, intended for human and machine use; every term has an identifier, standard metadata and logical definitions.
principles.evidence: An ontology is a system of carefully defined terminology, connected by logical relationships, and designed for both humans and computers to use. OBI is about scientific investigations, so OBI contains general terms such as ‘assay’ and specific terms such as ‘genotyping by high throughput sequencing assay’. Every term has a unique identifier, standard metadata, and logical definitions that connect it to other terms in OBI and the wider OBO community.

principles.principle: Search existing repositories before submitting a new term.
principles.evidence: Before you submit a new term, please search OntoBee or BioPortal for the term you want and its synonyms.

principles.principle: If you find a similar term but want changes, open a GitHub issue and include the term name, IRI, and description of requested changes and reasons.
principles.evidence: If you find a term that’s close enough, but would like additions or changes made to it, please submit a new ticket to our issue tracker and be sure to include: the name of the term in the title of the ticket the IRI that identifies the term (something like http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/OBI_0000070 ) a description of the changes you would like made and reasons for the changes

principles.principle: New term requests must supply specific metadata fields (editor preferred term, alternative terms, textual definition, definition source, logical definition/parent term, example of usage, term editor).
principles.evidence: If you don’t find the term you’re looking for, but it’s within OBI’s scope of biomedical investigations, please suggest that we add it to OBI as a new term. We’ll need the following information before we can add your term (more details below): editor preferred term: a unique, unambiguous label for the term in American English alternative terms: common synonyms or translations textual definition definition source for the textual definition logical definition (or parent term) example of usage term editor: your name, and that of any collaborators, as it should appear in OBI When you’ve collected as much of this information as possible, please follow this link to submit a term request to our tracker: https://github.com/obi-ontology/obi/issues/new (A GitHub account is required.)

principles.principle: The editor preferred term must be a single, unambiguous American-English label (no acronyms/jargon), unique within OBO Foundry.
principles.evidence: The editor preferred term is an unambiguous label that uniquely identifies the term within the OBO Foundry. There must be one and only one editor preferred term, and it must be in American English. It should not contain any acronyms or jargon words, and it should make sense when read outside the context of a scientific investigation.

principles.principle: Textual definitions are required, should follow Aristotelian form ('An A is a B that C'), be in American English, and be unique across the OBO Foundry.
principles.evidence: The textual definition is the most important annotation because it expresses the meaning of your term. Definitions should have Aristotelian form: “An A is a B that C” where A is your new term, B is the parent term, and C spells out how A is a special kind of B. Every term needs one and only one textual definition, in American English, and definitions must be unique across the OBO Foundry.

principles.principle: Every textual definition must include a definition source (author, URL or DOI as appropriate).
principles.evidence: Every textual definition should have a definition source. If you created the definition, then that source would be you, and we’ll record your name. If the definition was adapted from Wikipedia or some other website, then this annotation should contain the permanent URL. If it was adapted from a paper, use its DOI or PubMed URL.

principles.principle: Provide a logical definition (machine-readable) expressed in OWL2; most OBI terms are OWL classes and require a single parent class.
principles.evidence: The logical definition of a term is almost as important as the textual definition. I say “almost” because, in case of misunderstandings, the textual definition takes precedence. The logical definition expresses the meaning of the term in a machine-readable way using the Web Ontology Language (OWL) version 2. Most OBI terms are OWL Classes (i.e. general nouns) and every one of these requires a single parent class.

principles.principle: Include one or more example-of-usage annotations to clarify meaning; examples are strongly recommended though not strictly required.
principles.evidence: One or more example of usage annotations can really clarify the meaning of a term. While the textual definition must be general enough to cover all cases, the examples provide specific cases that show the term in action. Examples of usage can be common cases that demonstrate the prototypical usage, or uncommon edge cases that delimit the scope of the term. While not strictly required, every new term should have one or more examples of usage.

principles.principle: Provide 'term editor' annotations to credit contributors.
principles.evidence: Finally, we want to give you credit for your work. We will add one or more term editor annotations with your name, and the names of others who have collaborated on creating this term for OBI.

principles.principle: OBI adheres to OBO Foundry principles and uses IAO Ontology Metadata annotations for minimal term metadata.
principles.evidence: OBI belongs to the OBO Foundry and strives to follow the OBO Foundry Principles. We have rules for the minimal metadata for every term, and we use the IAO Ontology Metadata annotations for them.

principles.principle: For bulk term requests, use OBI's ROBOT/TSV templates (spreadsheet format) to standardize submissions; templates live in the repository.
principles.evidence: For large sets of new terms, we suggest using our term templates to standardize your requests. These exist in a spreadsheet format to allow for consistancy across a large number of new terms. Currently, there are termplates for assay, device, study design, and more. Templates can be found here https://github.com/obi-ontology/obi/tree/master/src/ontology/templates

principles.principle: OBI uses OntoFox for imports from external ontologies and ROBOT templates to convert spreadsheets to OWL; edit the specified input/template files in the repo when contributing.
principles.evidence: Our ontology terms come in three groups. ... 1. external terms (from other ontologies): We use OntoFox for imports. Edit the corresponding `src/ontology/OntoFox_inputs/` file. 2. template terms: We use ROBOT templates to convert spreadsheets to OWL. Edit the relevant `src/ontology/templates/` file: ... 3. other terms: Edit `src/ontology/obi-edit.owl` in Protege.

standards.notes: Extraction focused on OBI term guidelines, README and documentation pages. The source is an ontology/project web site and developer repository (prose guidance and templates), so content is represented as principles (requirements/recommendations) rather than a field-level metadata table or workflow DAG.

standards.name: IAO Ontology Metadata
standards.abstract: The materials are OWL/RDF ontology exports (OBO/OWL) that describe controlled vocabularies used to annotate biomedical and chemical investigations: classes (terms), annotation properties (e.g. definition), and hierarchical relationships (rdfs:subClassOf). The files include imports from established ontologies (GO, HP, CHMO, BAO, etc.) and JSON/OWL serializations intended for programmatic reuse. The ‘standard’ here is the representation of metadata using IAO/OBO-style annotation properties and OWL class hierarchies: maintained through the OBO ecosystem (IAO/OBI/ontologies such as CHMO, HPO, GO), it addresses the problem of providing consistent machine-readable metadata (labels, definitions, provenance, identifiers) for ontology terms used in biomedical investigations.

classification.rationale: The source files are OWL/RDF ontology serializations that define classes and explicit rdfs:subClassOf relationships (a hierarchical graph). This is a directed acyclic graph (ontology taxonomy) rather than a field-level metadata table or a prose checklist, e.g. many <owl:Class> entries and <rdfs:subClassOf> relations appear in the source.

standards.name: Web Ontology Language (OWL) — OWL 2
standards.abstract: The materials are a collection of OWL/XML ontology files, README and tool instructions showing OWL usage in practice. The research objects represented are ontologies (classes, properties, individuals and annotations) used to describe domain knowledge (for example nanomaterial safety assessment in the eNanoMapper project, chemical methods in CHMO, and chemical entities in ChEBI). The files are exchanged and stored in OWL/RDF serializations (RDF/XML shown) and are produced and consumed by tools such as the OWL API, Protégé and OntoFox. The 'standard' content in the seed material is not a tabular metadata schema but operational guidance and examples for creating, importing, annotating and using OWL ontologies; the files demonstrate common OWL constructs (owl:Ontology, owl:Class, rdfs:subClassOf, owl:imports, annotation properties) and practical notes about generating and editing OWL outputs.

classification.rationale: The source material is prose guidance plus example OWL files and README instructions (how-to and conventions). It does not present a row/column metadata table nor an ordered procedural DAG; instead it provides guidance and examples (instructions, policies, and annotated examples) — matching the 'principle' category.

principles.principle: OWL is used to represent ontologies and application ontologies for domain knowledge using semantic web standards.
principles.evidence: The eNanoMapper project (www.enanomapper.net) is creating a pan-European computational infrastructure for toxicological data management for ENMs, based on semantic web standards and ontologies. This ontology is an application ontology targeting the full domain of nanomaterial safety assessment. It re-uses several other ontologies including the NPO, CHEMINF, ChEBI, and ENVO.

principles.principle: Ontologies reuse other ontologies via owl:imports.
principles.evidence: <owl:imports rdf:resource="https://enanomapper.github.io/ontologies/external-dev/aopo-slim.owl"/>

principles.principle: OWL expresses classes and subclass relationships using <owl:Class> and <rdfs:subClassOf>.
principles.evidence:
<owl:Class rdf:about="http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/CHEBI_145810">
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/CHEBI_16670"/>
        <rdfs:subClassOf rdf:resource="http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/CHEBI_33839"/>
        <obo:IAO_0000111>insulin</obo:IAO_0000111>
        <obo:IAO_0000115>A peptide hormone which consists of two polypeptide chains, A- and B- chains which are linked together by disulfide bonds. The amino acid sequence of insulin varies across species and certain segments of the molecule are highly conserved. In most species, the A chain consists of 21 amino acids and the B chain consists of 30 amino acids. In mammals, insulin is synthesised in the pancreas within the β cells whereas in certain species of fish, the insulin-producing tissue is uniquely located in separate structures called Brockmann bodies.</obo:IAO_0000115>
        <obo:IAO_0000412 rdf:resource="http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/chebi.owl"/>
        <rdfs:label>insulin</rdfs:label>
    </owl:Class>

principles.principle: OWL uses annotation properties to provide labels and textual definitions for terms.
principles.evidence:
<owl:AnnotationProperty rdf:about="http://purl.obolibrary.org/obo/IAO_0000115">
        <obo:IAO_0000111>definition</obo:IAO_0000111>
        <obo:IAO_0000111 xml:lang="en">definition</obo:IAO_0000111>
        <obo:IAO_0000111>textual definition</obo:IAO_0000111>
        <obo:IAO_0000115>A property representing the English language definitions of what NCI means by the concept. They may also include information about the definition's source and attribution in a form that can easily be interpreted by software.</obo:IAO_0000115>
        <rdfs:label>definition</rdfs:label>
    </owl:AnnotationProperty>

principles.principle: Practical processing advice: when using OntoFox to create instance-style outputs for ontologies that should be individuals (e.g., UO instance output), post-process the OWL to convert imported classes to NamedIndividuals and change subclass relations to rdf:type assertions.
principles.evidence:
Go to section "2. Data input using local text file:", upload OntoFox input file and then save the output OWL file

For UO instance output, following modification need to be made:
	replace 'owl:Class' by 'owl:NamedIndividual' of imported terms (not their parent classes)
	replace 'rdfs:subClassOf' by 'rdf:type'

principles.principle: Users can open OWL ontology files in Protégé directly from a URL using 'Open from URL' and the ontology web address.
principles.evidence:
Opening the ontology in Protégé
===============================

The stable version can be opened in [Protégé](https://protege.stanford.edu/) with the following step:

1. File → Open from URL...
2. enter the URL http://enanomapper.github.io/ontologies/enanomapper.owl

standards.notes: Extracted principles are based on example OWL files and README/tool instructions included in the provided materials. The source material is a set of example ontologies and documentation rather than a formal specification document; the items above reflect recurring practical conventions and explicit instructions found in those files.
